content:
Open a bank account for your church when you are ready to receive and spend church funds. Use a dedicated organizational account to keep those transactions separate from your personal finances.

Before you apply, gather the church's legal documents and EIN, compare account terms, and involve your Financial Leader. Follow the church's existing financial-accountability policy when choosing who will use the account.

---

## Start with the church's financial controls

Read [Principles of Financial Accountability](/wiki/administrative/financial/principles-of-financial-accountability) before naming signers or requesting online access. It assigns financial operations to a Financial Leader under the elders' direction and keeps the Senior Pastor out of handling money, writing checks, and bank account access.

Ask the Financial Leader to carry those responsibilities into the account setup. Use the existing policy for separation of duties and spending approvals. Do not give someone transaction access simply because the application asks for information about that person.

<Callout type="scripture">
*"for we respect what is good, not only in the sight of the Lord, but also in the sight of men."* — 2 Corinthians 8:21 (LSB)
</Callout>

---

## Compare the account's actual costs

Ask prospective banks for the current account terms and fee schedule. The Small Business Administration recommends comparing transaction fees, minimum-balance fees, and early-termination fees rather than choosing your personal bank automatically.

Use this list when you speak with a banker:

| Ask about | What to confirm |
|---|---|
| Monthly costs | Maintenance fees and conditions for avoiding them |
| Balance requirements | Opening deposit and any ongoing minimum balance |
| Deposits and payments | Included transactions and charges after the allowance |
| Cash deposits | How the bank measures its allowance and charges for additional deposits |
| Online access | Separate user accounts and the permissions available |

A nonprofit account can have transaction and cash-deposit allowances even when it has no monthly maintenance fee. Ask the banker to explain both the headline offer and its disclosures before you choose.

<Callout type="important">
Bank terms and federal guidance were checked on October 15, 2026. Confirm current costs and application requirements with your bank, EIN confirmation options with the IRS, customer-identification guidance with FinCEN, and deposit-insurance limits with the FDIC before relying on them.
</Callout>

---

## Get the bank's document checklist

Tell the banker your church's legal structure before requesting a checklist. Requirements for a corporation can differ from those for an unincorporated association. Ask which documents establish the church's existence and which people must participate in opening the account.

Prepare the documents your bank requests:

- [ ] The church's EIN and any required IRS confirmation.
- [ ] Formation documents, such as articles of incorporation, a charter, or articles of association, as applicable.
- [ ] Government-issued identification and personal information for authorized signers.
- [ ] Any required assumed-name documentation if the church uses a different public name.
- [ ] Any additional evidence of current officers or authority requested for the church's structure.

For example, Chase's unincorporated-association checklist includes organizational documents and may require meeting minutes listing current officers. Treat that as a bank-specific example, not a universal church checklist.

---

## Bring the right EIN evidence

The IRS says you can use a newly assigned EIN immediately to open a bank account. Ask your bank what written confirmation it accepts.

If you need confirmation, the IRS lists an entity transcript, a digital CP575 for eligible Business Tax Account users, and Letter 147C, EIN Previously Assigned. Request Letter 147C through the IRS business and specialty tax line. The digital CP575 can substitute for the original CP575A-J notice series and Letter 147C.

When preparing the application, compare the church name on the EIN record with its formation documents. The IRS instructs applicants to use the name on their registration or formation documents when applying for an EIN.

<Callout type="tip">
If you already have an EIN, use the IRS confirmation process when documentation is missing. Do not apply for another EIN just to replace a missing notice.
</Callout>

---

## Expect questions about the people involved

FinCEN distinguishes nonprofit ownership from control. A nonprofit or nonstock corporation, or similar entity validly organized with the appropriate state authority, is excluded from the ownership part of the customer-due-diligence requirement. That exclusion does not depend on federal tax-exempt status. For a church organized as a nonprofit or nonstock corporation, the bank still collects information under the control part.

For such a corporation, expect to identify a person with significant responsibility for managing or directing the organization. FinCEN's examples include a treasurer. Its guidance calls for identifying information such as name, date of birth, address, and Social Security number or another applicable government identification number.

FinCEN does not treat an unincorporated association as a legal entity customer, so this beneficial-ownership requirement does not apply. The bank still identifies signers and may ask for current officers under its own procedures. Explain the church's actual structure rather than inventing ownership percentages. Ask the banker to distinguish identity information from account permissions, and continue to follow the church's signer policy.

---

## Check how deposit insurance applies

For a qualifying corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association, FDIC coverage is up to $250,000 at the same insured bank. The organization must engage in an independent activity, meaning a legitimate purpose rather than existing solely to increase deposit-insurance coverage. Corporations and partnerships must also be validly formed under applicable state law.

The FDIC combines accounts owned by the same nonprofit corporation at the same bank. Calling one account an operating account and another a building fund does not give each its own insurance limit.

<Callout type="warning">
Do not count a separate insurance allowance for every account or fund name. If the church expects deposits beyond the applicable coverage, ask the FDIC and your bank to confirm how the church's ownership and account arrangement affect coverage.
</Callout>

---

## Complete the application with the banker

Confirm who must attend or complete identification steps before scheduling the appointment. Bring the requested documents and the required opening deposit. Review the information you submit against those documents.

Be prepared to describe the church's activities and expected account use. Bank applications may ask about the nature of the organization and the types and volume of transactions you expect. Give the banker the church's own information, including any additional details requested for its legal structure.

---

## Set up access for the approved roles

Ask the bank to show your Financial Leader how to configure each approved user's access. For example, U.S. Bank's Shared Access provides individual usernames and passwords, view-only access, and transaction access. Its administrators can add or remove users.

Check each permission against your church's financial-accountability policy before assigning it. Review who can see statements and who can move money. Follow [Disbursements and Approvals](/wiki/administrative/financial/disbursements-and-approvals) for the church's payment process, including its separation between initiating and approving online payments.

Use your bank's access reports to review users, permissions, and limits. Update access when authorized responsibilities change, and keep the church's payment documentation in its accounting records.

title: Opening the Church Bank Account

sources.quote: You can use your EIN immediately for most business needs. For example, when you: […] Open a bank account […] When you apply for an EIN, enter your business name as it appears on your registration or formation documents. […] A business entity should have only one EIN.

sources.claim: Section 4: confirmation routes and exact notice names, including eligibility limit for Business Tax Account users; bank acceptance is a question, not a guarantee.
sources.quote: Request an Entity transcript. […] Eligible Business Tax Account users can download a digital CP575, Employer Identification Number Verification Notice in BTA. […] It can be used as a substitute for the original CP575A-J notice series and Letter 147C, EIN Previously Assigned. […] Call our business and specialty tax line. […] Request Letter 147C, EIN Previously Assigned.

sources.claim: Section 5: nonprofit ownership exclusion has a state-organization condition, does not rely on IRC exemption, and retains control information collection; as of 2026-10-15, FAQ E.6 updated May 6, 2026.
sources.quote: The Rule does not rely on the tax-exempt status of an entity as described in the IRC. All nonprofit entities—whether or not tax-exempt—that are established as a nonprofit, or nonstock corporation, or similar entity that has been validly organized with the proper State authority are excluded from the ownership/equity prong of the requirement because nonprofit entities generally do not have ownership interests. Financial institutions, however, are required to collect beneficial ownership information under the control prong from any such entity.

sources.claim: Section 5: unincorporated associations are not legal entity customers under FinCEN CDD FAQ E.4, updated May 6, 2026, so the beneficial-ownership requirement does not apply.
sources.quote: Sole proprietorships—individual or spousal—and unincorporated associations are not legal entity customers as defined by the Rule

sources.claim: Section 5: control-person role and identifying details; stricter bank procedures permitted. Identity provision does not instruct the church to grant bank permissions.
sources.quote: A single individual with significant responsibility to control, manage, or direct a legal entity customer, including an executive officer or senior manager (e.g., a Chief Executive Officer, Chief Financial Officer, Chief Operating Officer, Managing Member, General Partner, President, Vice President, or Treasurer)

sources.claim: Section 5: names, birth dates, address and applicable identification number; no invented equity percentages for qualifying nonprofits.
sources.quote: the name, date of birth, address, and social security number or other government identification number (passport number or other similar information in the case of foreign persons)

sources.claim: Section 5: bank procedures may ask for more than the regulatory minimum.
sources.quote: Covered financial institutions may choose to implement stricter written internal policies and procedures for the collection and verification of beneficial ownership information than the requirements prescribed by the CDD Rule.

sources.claim: Section 6: exact insurance limit and eligibility; opened directly with Python HTTP client when web extraction failed. Amount and current guidance checked 2026-10-15.
sources.quote: The deposit accounts of a corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association are insured for up to $250,000, provided the corporation, partnership, or unincorporated association is engaged in an "independent activity". […] The term "independent activity" means that the entity is operated primarily for a legitimate business purpose and not solely to increase deposit insurance coverage. […] Corporations and partnerships must be validly formed under the applicable state law to receive insurance coverage that is separate from any coverage that the owners, officers, or partners of the business might otherwise receive.

sources.claim: Section 6: same nonprofit corporation accounts at the same bank aggregate despite differing fund purposes; confirm arrangement with FDIC and bank.
sources.quote: Accounts held by the same non-profit corporation, but designated for different purposes, are not insured separately. All of the accounts held in the name of a non-profit corporation are added together and insured for up to $250,000.

sources.claim: Section 8 and comparison table: bank example offers separate credentials, view-only versus transaction permissions, administrator user changes and reports of users/access/limits. Confirm chosen bank supports needed controls.
